'Refresh' is the right term, but triggers are not the standard mechanism. Disk/SSD holds the bulk of CDN cache, but CDNs also keep hot content in RAM. Fastly, for example, runs 384 GB RAM plus 6 TB SSD per cache server and uses algorithms to keep commonly used data in RAM. (The teacher hedged.)
precise_version: CDN servers use tiered caching: the most frequently requested objects are kept in RAM and the long tail on SSD.

note: SSDs are not close to RAM in latency: a main-memory reference is about 100 ns, while a random 4 KB SSD read is about 150 µs, roughly 1000x slower (sequential reads close the gap to about 4x). Being near users doesn't remove the benefit of RAM for hot objects.
precise_version: SSDs are fast compared with network and spinning disks but still orders of magnitude slower than RAM for random reads, which is why CDNs keep hot objects in memory and the rest on SSD.

note: The student's RAM, then disk, then origin model is broadly how CDN cache tiers work; CDNs do keep hot user content (not just configuration) in RAM.

Rate limiting mitigates some application-layer (L7) floods but does not handle volumetric or infrastructure-layer DDoS. UDP reflection and SYN floods saturate network capacity before an application-layer limiter ever sees them. AWS says mitigation requires capacity that scales faster than the flood, to absorb or filter it upstream (CDN/anycast scrubbing, AWS Shield, Cloudflare).
precise_version: Rate limiting is one layer of DDoS defense, effective against some L7 request floods. Volumetric L3/L4 attacks must be absorbed or filtered upstream by providers with enough network capacity (CDN/anycast scrubbing services).

note: Standard primary defense is parameterized queries / safe stored procedures (OWASP). 'Know exactly how to patch CVEs' is optimistic but fine as a deferral.

Not every vendor cluster is sharded. Oracle RAC, the student's example, is shared-disk: multiple instances access a single set of database files on shared storage, so data is not split across nodes. Shared-nothing clusters (MongoDB sharded clusters, Vitess) do shard.
precise_version: Database clusters are either shared-nothing (data sharded across nodes, e.g. MongoDB sharded clusters, Vitess) or shared-disk (e.g. Oracle RAC, where several instances share one copy of the data on shared storage).

note: The line isn't paid vs open source. Many open-source systems shard natively (MongoDB, Cassandra, Vitess for MySQL, Citus for PostgreSQL). Stock MySQL and PostgreSQL are the main cases where you shard in the application or add a layer.
precise_version: Whether you must shard yourself depends on the database: plain MySQL/PostgreSQL need app-level sharding or an add-on (Vitess, Citus); natively distributed databases, open source or paid, handle it.

Single-document operations in MongoDB were always atomic. Multi-document ACID transactions came in 4.0 for replica sets and 4.2 for sharded clusters. The conclusion (don't say 'MongoDB has no ACID') is correct.

The trend is real (MySQL has a native JSON type; PostgreSQL has json/jsonb; Hudi publishes commits atomically). But 'wide-column stores support ACID' overstates it: Cassandra offers Paxos-based lightweight transactions (compare-and-set) and atomic batches, and is otherwise eventually consistent. 'Because building is easy' is opinion.
precise_version: Databases are converging on features (JSON in relational DBs, transactions in MongoDB and data lakes), but guarantees still differ: Cassandra, for example, has only lightweight compare-and-set transactions, not general ACID.
